title: God is simple (ST I.3)
hookLine: God has no parts; his being and his essence are one

lines: A RADIO ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.
cards: A kid with a screwdriver has the back off an old radio on the kitchen floor. Screws in a saucer. A circuit board.
A speaker cone. Wires in four colors. He's learning what grown-ups know: open almost anything and you find pieces.
A sandwich is pieces. A song is notes. A sentence is words.
You are a body and a breath, habits and moods, a past and a plan. So here's the question Thomas Aquinas asks right after the five ways: if God is, what is God made of? His answer is today's word.

teach.h: WE KNOW WHAT GOD IS NOT.
teach.b: Thomas opens with a confession: we can't know what God is, only what God is not. So he works by taking things away.

teach.h: NO BODY, NO PIECES, NO ADD-ONS.
teach.b: First, a body. God is not one. He leans on Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is a spirit."
Then further: God isn't made of anything at all. No stuff plus shape. No pieces.
And no add-ons. You have a good habit, maybe patience, but you are not your patience; you could lose it on a bad Monday and still be you.

teach.h: WHAT GOD IS, IS TO BE.
teach.b: There's a gap between who you are and what you have. In God, Thomas says, there's no gap. God doesn't have goodness the way you have patience.
Then the deepest step. For everything else, what it is and that it is are two different things. You can know what a unicorn is without it existing.
Your being is lent. In God, Thomas says, the two are one: what God is, is to be. Why care?
Because anything made of parts depends on its parts, and on whatever put them together.

A God built of pieces would need a builder, and the first cause of the five ways can't be like that. So simplicity here doesn't mean plain, or easy to understand; Thomas reaches it the hard way, by saying what God is not.
It means whole. Undivided. Nothing in God pulling against anything else in God.
Some readers find that strange and cold at first. Others find it a rest. On Thomas's account, a God with no parts is a God who can't come apart.

how: Catholic theology teaches divine simplicity as part of the doctrine of God, and readers of the Summa meet it right after the five ways, in the Summa's third question.

o: God's having no parts: whole, not put together
God being plain, easy for anyone to understand
a life of few things, free of clutter and fuss

p: something you have, and can lose

s: for Thomas, 'simple' means God is easy to understand
it means not made of parts; Thomas says we grasp it by saying what God is not.
Thomas says that in God, what God is and that God is are one
for everything else they are two; God's being is not lent.
Thomas says God has goodness the way a person has a good habit
a person can gain or lose a habit; in God, Thomas says, there's no gap between who God is and what God has.

games.q: a child asks Thomas: what is God made of? which is closest to his answer?
o: the finest, lightest stuff there is.
nothing: God isn't made of parts at all.
games.why: Thomas says God has no body, no stuff plus shape, no add-ons: anything made of parts would depend on them and need a builder.

practice: Choose one thing only, a single breath, a candle flame, a smooth stone in your palm, and let everything else fall to the edges. When your mind starts taking it apart, naming, comparing, planning, come back to the one thing, whole.
If you pray, rest there before the God Thomas calls simple; if you don't, just stay with the one thing.

wordCard.voice: Simplicity. In Thomas Aquinas, not plainness but wholeness: God has no parts, and in God what God is and that God is are one.

orig.note: Latin: simplicity, being uncomposed — Thomas's word for God having no parts.

carryVoice: Your line: no parts. Tomorrow, how anyone can talk about a God like that. Rest well.

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 3 (prologue and articles 1–7)
